newsitem.title: USA: Japan's shrinking trade surplus boosts dollar against yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan's shrinking trade surplus boosts dollar against yen.

text.p: The dollar rose against the Japanese yen Friday in response to new reports on trade balances, but declined against other major currencies.

Most of the dollar's gains against the yen were posted in overnight trading on foreign markets after Japan's Ministry of Finance reported the Japanese trade surplus tumbled 30.3 percent to 779.52 billion yen in September from a year earlier.
The smaller Japanese trade surplus tends to support the dollar because Japanese firms will have fewer dollars to convert back into yen.
In U.S. trading, the dollar held those gains but came under pressure against other major currencies after U.S. trade data was released, showing a bigger trade deficit than expected.
The August deficit in the U.S. trade balance capped the dollar's rise against the yen and sent the dollar lower against the German mark, dealers said.
The dollar closed at 112.53 yen, up from 112.20 yen late Thursday. Against the mark, the dollar ended at 1.5424 compared to 1.5430 late Thursday.
Economists had expected a significant contraction in the U.S. trade numbers after the gap ballooned in July to $11.60 billion, the highest monthly shortfall since the end of 1987.
An increase in imported Chinese Christmas decorations and toys boosted the overall August trade gap to $10.83 billion, exceeding the consensus forecast for an $8.4 billion shortfall.
"The dollar sold off originally against the mark in particular because the trade number was a disappointment," said Tom Benfer, director of foreign exchange at the Bank of Montreal in New York.
"But it didn't really have a strong and lasting impact on the dollar," he added.
The British pound surged against the mark to a 22-month high at 2.4568.
In late trade, the dollar held firm after news Russian President Boris Yeltsin fired a second top-ranking official in his government.
Yeltsin dismissed Russian armed forces chief of staff Gen. Mikhail Kolesnikov, a long-serving career officer who served as caretaker defence minister for a month this year.
Kolesnikov had no known links with former security chief Alexander Lebed, whom Yeltsin dismissed Thursday in an attempt to crush an escalating Kremlin power struggle.

The dollar surged against the mark Thursday after Lebed's dismissal. The mark typically suffers from political instability in Russia given Germany's geographical proximity and economic links with the country.

"I figured there would be a reaction to Kolesnikov, but nothing much happened. We had much more of a reaction yesterday to Lebed's firing. It's Friday afternoon and people have squared up positions already for the weekend," said Jay Wertheimer, senior currency trader at Banco di Sicilia.
In other trade, sterling gained to $1.5887 from $1.5875 in late Thursday trade. The dollar rose to 1.2704 Swiss francs from 1.2693 on Thursday and fell to Canadian $1.3491 from C$1.3524.
